rv.q: Ms. Ziegler’s drama, perfectly cast in a superlative Roundabout Theatre Company production from director Barry Edelstein, handily ranks as the finest play of the admittedly young new year.
It’s an impressive construction, but we see the scaffolding a little too clearly, hinting at missed opportunity.
Anna Ziegler’s awkwardly hitched play “The Wanderers,” which opened Thursday at the Laura Pels Theater, may be the first to consider the problem of forced matches while also exemplifying it.

You don’t have to be Jewish to get a little verklempt at this point — or to appreciate the eloquence, insight, and deeply humane vision that Ms. Ziegler applies to her wanderers on their disparate journeys.
Ziegler has written a beautifully shaded portrait of two generations of Brooklyn marriages, and truthfully, you should be drawn in.
"The Wanderers" lasts only 105 minutes without intermission, and yet effectively holds enough storylines for a half dozen lesser plays.
And in “The Wanderers,” she collaborates with the well-cast performers and director Barry Edelstein in creating five absorbing characters.
Anna Ziegler’s new play is a sly and moving drama looking at marriage, parents, children and the things we inherit and reject – religion, tradition, fear and dreams.
Two marriages unravel, spectacularly, in The Wanderers, and you're likely to care much more about one than the other.
While the play is not as detailed as it might be in all respects, it is always absorbing, while not as heartfelt as it might be.
Still, there is a slight sense of flatness that this revolving door of paired scenes creates within a play whose ideas are bursting with three-dimensionality.
I imagine your mileage may vary.

It’s a compelling construct that tries its best to hold Anna Ziegler's ambitious story together but somehow muddles itself in its own high-mindedness and poor formulation.

cn.t: Ziegler's literary drama about two Brooklyn Jewish couples across generations draws mixed reviews. Critics praise its intelligence and late-play twist, but many find it tedious and overly contrived, with characters that feel more like authorial constructs than believable people.
